demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'Feels Present Not Past' and 'Full Sensory Reliving' indicate highly intrusive, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' These can sometimes coexist, but stated this strongly they pull in opposite directions and are hard to reconcile as the same memory profile.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The Threat items depict pervasive fear of being physically attacked by other people ('watch other people closely', 'back to wall', 'stay alert at night'), which does not fit well with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. For this trauma, threat is more plausibly guilt, condemnation, or fear of consequences, not generalized interpersonal danger.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Mirror Checking' is not well linked to the rest of the profile. Nothing in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Negative Appraisals suggests appearance-focused concern, dissociation needing visual reassurance, or checking for injury; as selected, it appears clinically disconnected.

Mirror checking is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; it more strongly suggests concerns about visible injury, appearance, or being followed, none of which are supported by the other nodes.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Back-to-wall hypervigilance and scanning the room imply an interpersonal or attack-related threat context. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which centers on guilt, reliving, and self-blame after accidentally injuring someone rather than danger from other people.

vignette:
Marcus Heller, a 34-year-old White American school counselor, presented for his initial intake appointment approximately fourteen months after the event that he described, with visible effort, as the worst moment of his life. He is married and, by his own account, has spent the better part of the past year trying to ensure that his wife and colleagues never fully understand what he carries.

The incident occurred on a Saturday afternoon in late autumn when Marcus was driving home from a school district professional development conference. He was fatigued and, by his own admission, had been managing a persistent headache all day. On a two-lane rural highway, he drifted partially into the oncoming lane. The driver of the approaching vehicle swerved hard to avoid a head-on collision, lost control, and struck a guardrail. Marcus pulled over immediately. When he reached the other car, he found a man in his fifties slumped against the steering wheel, unresponsive, his face lacerated and his arm bent at an angle that made clear something was badly broken. Marcus called 911 and knelt beside the man, pressing his jacket against the wound on the man's forehead. What he has never been able to fully articulate - what seems to stop his speech entirely when he approaches it - is the smell: engine fluid, blood, and something sharper underneath, something he cannot name and cannot forget. The man survived but sustained a traumatic brain injury and required months of inpatient rehabilitation. Marcus was not charged with any offense. He was told, repeatedly, that it was an accident. He has never believed it.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus found himself replaying the moment of impact - not as a memory he could observe from a distance, but as something immediate and total. When it came, it arrived with the full weight of sensation: the sound of the other car hitting the guardrail, the cold of the pavement under his knees, and above all that smell, which had no clean translation into language but which he recognized instantly whenever something approximated it - a hospital antiseptic, a particular kind of cleaning solvent used in the school's maintenance closet, gasoline at a filling station. Each time, his body responded as though the event were unfolding in the present moment: his heart rate spiked, his hands trembled, and he was briefly unable to locate himself in time.

He had come to believe, with quiet certainty, that he was not a person who could be trusted to act correctly when it mattered. This belief had taken on particular weight in his professional life. As a school counselor, Marcus regularly encounters students in distress, and what had once felt like a natural competence now felt like a performance conducted over a void. He had begun keeping his mind relentlessly occupied - reviewing student case notes, listening to podcasts during every commute, filling silences at home with television - because stillness was when the memory arrived uninvited. He avoided thinking about the event directly, and he had developed a careful habit of rerouting his drives to avoid passing the stretch of highway where it happened, which added nearly twenty minutes to his commute each day.

When a routine physical was scheduled last spring, Marcus cancelled it twice. The thought of a medical examination - the clinical smell of the room, the procedural handling of his body - produced a dread he could not explain to his wife without telling her more than he was prepared to say. He had also stopped taking a shortcut near the local police precinct, uncertain of what he felt when he saw a patrol car but knowing that whatever it was, it was not manageable in public.

His wife had noticed the distance. She had named it, gently and then less gently, over several months. It was ultimately her quiet statement - that she felt she was living with someone who had decided to disappear - that brought Marcus to the referral. He arrived at intake exhausted, guarded, and carrying the particular shame of a man who helps others process difficulty for a living and has been unable to apply any of that to himself. What he feared most was confirming what he already suspected: that the accident had not merely changed him, but had revealed something about him that had always been true.
